content: Austin Flint's examination did not directly compare the effects of the active treatment and the placebo within the same trial. However, this approach marked a significant deviation from the prevailing medical practice of the time, which typically involved contrasting the outcomes of an active treatment with what Flint referred to as the natural history of disease. To assess the moral and therapeutic impact of a treatment specifically administered for a disease, Flint placed patients on a placebo regimen. This placebo was primarily a highly diluted tincture of quassia, which was administered regularly. In Flint's wards, this placebo became widely recognized as the placeboic remedy for rheumatism. Flint treated 13 hospital patients diagnosed with rheumatic fever, of whom 11 had acute cases and 2 had sub-acute cases. He then compared the outcomes of his placebo treatment with the already well-documented results of the active treatment, which he had previously tested and reported on in earlier studies. In 1946, following World War II, there was a shortage of pharmaceutical chemicals. A manufacturer of a headache remedy, which consisted of three ingredients (a, b, and c), faced a scarcity of ingredient b. The manufacturer requested Jellinek to investigate whether the absence of ingredient b would compromise the overall efficacy of the drug. Jellinek designed a complex trial involving 199 participants who suffered from frequent headaches (initially 200 participants were enrolled, but one did not complete the trial). The participants were randomly divided into four test groups. Jellinek prepared four test drugs, each representing different combinations of the three ingredients, along with a placebo as a scientific control. This trial was notable because, at the time, placebos were primarily used to measure the relative efficacy of a drug by determining how much better the drug performed compared to the placebo. The trial conducted by Austin Flint is an example of such a drug efficacy versus placebo efficacy study. The four test drugs were identical in appearance, size, color, and taste: Drug A: Contained ingredients a, b, and c. Drug B: Contained ingredients a and c. Drug C: Contained ingredients a and b. Drug D: A simulator, contained only ordinary lactate. Each time a participant experienced a headache, they took the test drug assigned to their group and recorded whether their headache was relieved or not.
